source.title: Limitations on the Interpretability of Learned Features from Sparse Dictionary Learning

record.file_problem: none; full post text is present
record.tranche_reason: The post gives a specific theoretical argument that a single extracted feature need not correspond one-to-one with an ideally interpretable feature: a continuous feature's output effect may require multiple coupled model features. It does not test this on trained models or real SAE features.
record.gate_note: The results are mathematical analyses of hypothetical binary and continuous features in a single-layer model, not measurements on a trained model. The post also mentions reported findings from Towards Monosemanticity, but those are cited background and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A theoretical post with no trained model or SAE. It explicitly assumes superposition theory fully dictates representations and that SAE features equal the model's true features. It then argues that linear-logit constraints can force one human-interpretable data feature to be split across several coupled model features. That is a claim about how data-generating features map to model features and how interpretable they are. It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units (V5). It does not test any other version either. The record's T5 tests/V5 reading overstates it.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author argues, as self-described weak evidence, that architectural constraints can split a continuous idealized feature across coupled model features. Individual SAE features could thus be accurate yet uninterpretable in isolation, and shallower models might need more features per idealized feature. Relevance to real datasets is left open.
record.recipe_differences: A theoretical analysis of softmax/logit constraints in hypothetical single-layer models, rather than a reproduction of the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The result depends on whether the idealized feature is binary or continuous, and on whether one or multiple coupled model features are available.

fits_no_version.finding: In a hypothetical single-layer model with linear logit effects, one feature cannot represent a continuous idealized feature with non-monotonic token-probability ratios. Two or more coupled features can represent it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural constraints can force one interpretable data-generating variable to be split into several coupled model or SAE features, so individual features may be accurate yet uninterpretable in isolation.

record.problems: The examples are contrived and hypothetical; the post does not test the argument on trained models or real datasets, and it characterizes its evidence as weak.

untested.parts: No toy-model training, geometry, or sparsity transition.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions.
SAE completeness, stability and canonicality are assumed, not tested; no SAE is trained.
Features are assumed to be linear 1-D directions; the coupled-feature idea is not tested as multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The record treats an assumption-laden thought experiment as a test of V5. The post takes SAE features to equal the model's true features ('any results below can be applied to either') and argues only about their interpretability relative to idealized data features. Its mention of 'token in context' features is cited from Towards Monosemanticity, not a result of this post.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The post does not test whether neurons become polysemantic because features compete for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The post discusses interpretability and feature-to-feature mapping, but does not test polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence for superposition.
No real LLM feature distribution or SAE recovery of sparse features is measured.
The argument concerns whether a single SAE/model feature can fully correspond to an idealized feature. It does not empirically test SAE completeness, stability, or canonicality on real models.
The post does not test the geometry of superposition or whether the features that are superposed are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: single-layer model (hypothetical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives whether one linear-logit feature can represent the output effect of a binary idealized feature.

conditions.value: three active tokens in fixed ratios

rows.measure: Representability of the idealized feature's output distribution by one model feature
rows.value: A single linear feature can exactly fit any arbitrary fixed distribution over the three tokens.
rows.note: The post's mathematical example is hypothetical; it is not a result on a trained model or an SAE.
rows.check: A derivation for a hypothetical binary feature, not a measurement. It concerns whether a linear feature can fit an idealized feature's output distribution, not whether SAE features are canonical model units.

rows.subject: single-layer model (hypothetical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the probability-ratio functions available to one linear-logit feature for a continuous idealized feature.
rows.measure: Whether one model feature can represent the idealized feature's output effect
rows.value: Probability ratios from one feature must be monotonic over the activation domain; it cannot always represent the idealized feature's output effect.
rows.note: This is a theoretical limitation derived for the constructed example, not an empirical measure of SAE features.
rows.check: A derivation showing one linear-logit feature gives only monotonic probability ratios. It is a construct outside every version; 'partial' has no version effect to measure against.

rows.subject: single-layer model (hypothetical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the output probability ratios when two model features fire together for one continuous idealized feature.
rows.measure: Whether coupled model features can represent non-monotonic probability ratios
rows.baseline: one feature cannot always represent the output effect
rows.value: Two or more coupled features can represent ratios that decrease over one domain and increase over another; one idealized feature is thereby mapped to multiple internal features.
rows.note: The post presents this as a theoretical representational possibility, not an observed trained-model result.
rows.check: A derivation that coupled features can fit non-monotonic ratios. It assumes SAE features equal the model's features rather than testing it, so it bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The derivation shows that one internal feature may be insufficient to represent an idealized feature's full output effect, while coupled features can be needed; this qualifies one-to-one interpretations of individual features. This is not an empirical test of SAE completeness or stability (r2, r3).
